what_it_does: AMD's Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV) is a feature that encrypts the memory of a virtual machine so that the cloud provider's software — or another tenant's virtual machine — cannot read it. This paper shows two previously unknown ways to spy on a protected virtual machine even without breaking the encryption. The first is a side channel based on timing how long it takes to flush a set of cache lines (the fast on-chip storage that holds recently used memory): because the timing varies depending on which addresses the victim has recently used, an attacker can infer the victim's memory access pattern. The second is a side channel based on memory contention: when two programs compete for access to the same memory bank at the same time, the slower one's timing leaks information about what the faster one is doing. The researchers use these two channels to build a practical attack that extracts a 128-bit AES encryption key from a victim virtual machine running under AMD's strongest SEV-SNP protection mode.
